target.task: Our university makerspace buys nine kinds of consumables. Annual spend last year (BDT): PLA filament 180,000; resin 110,000; acrylic sheet 52,000; solder wire 21,000; sandpaper 13,000; glue sticks 9,000; zip ties 6,500; fire blanket 5,000; eye-wash cartridges 3,500. Two technicians share stock checks, and checking everything weekly takes too long. Decide how often each item is checked.

rules.text: Give every one of the nine items exactly one check frequency: weekly, monthly or quarterly.
At most 3 items may be checked weekly.
Explain the method in method_summary in at most 40 words.

target.format: Reply with JSON only, in this shape: {"items": [{"item": "PLA filament", "frequency": "weekly, monthly or quarterly"}], "method_summary": "..."}

source_example.text: ABC analysis is a standard way to decide how much attention each stock item deserves. It is usually credited to H. Ford Dickie of General Electric, who described it in 1951 under the slogan "shoot for dollars, not pennies". The method rests on the Pareto pattern: a few items account for most of the money spent. A typical textbook example is a hardware wholesaler with ten stock items. The wholesaler first lists each item's annual spend in US dollars, for example 60,000 dollars for door hinges and 300 dollars for rubber washers. It then sorts the items from the largest annual spend to the smallest. Next it adds up the spend item by item and works out the running share of the total. An item is class A if the running share, including that item, is at most 80 percent. It is class B if the running share is above 80 and at most 95 percent. All remaining items are class C. In the example, two items, hinges and deadbolts, make up 78 percent of spend and become class A. Four items make up the next 16 percent and become class B. The last four items, including washers and wall plugs, share the final 6 percent and become class C. Class A items are counted every week in a cycle count, class B items every month and class C items once a quarter. The wholesaler also sets tighter reorder points for class A items and orders them more often in smaller lots. Class C items are ordered in large lots twice a year, because their total value is small. Managers like the method because it is simple and needs only one number per item. Its known weakness is that annual spend is the only criterion. A cheap item can still be critical, for example a spare part whose absence stops a machine. Some firms therefore add a criticality class or move critical items up by hand. Silver, Pyke and Thomas describe the method and these refinements in their textbook on inventory management.
